issues.description: The problem statement and UML refer to a Stock class (and specify that SealSaloon.stock should be of type Stock), but the provided template implements the inventory functionality in a class named Inventory and leaves Stock.java empty. The solution implementation uses Inventory (SealSaloon declares a static Inventory stock) instead of Stock. This naming/type mismatch between 'Stock' (spec in the problem/UML) and 'Inventory' (template & solution) is structural and will confuse students about which class to use/modify and whether they must implement Stock or Inventory.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the naming consistent across all artifacts. Either (A) rename the template's Inventory class to Stock (updating file and references) so it matches the problem statement and UML, or (B) update the problem statement and UML to refer to Inventory instead of Stock. Alternatively, provide a Stock class implementation that delegates to or wraps Inventory and update the template Stock.java accordingly. Ensure SealSaloon.stock is declared with the same type as the class provided in the template/UML.

issues.description: The problem statement and UML refer to a class named 'Stock' (and a 'stock' attribute of type Stock) while the provided template and the reference solution use a class named 'Inventory' to represent the same conceptual entity and expose the same methods (add, take, findStockIngredient, addToStockIngredients, emptyStock). This mismatch between 'Stock' and 'Inventory' can confuse students who will look for a 'Stock' class to modify or instantiate, making the mapping from the problem description to the code less direct.
issues.suggestedFix: Unify the identifier for the shared stock entity across all artifacts. Either rename the Inventory class/file to Stock (change class name to 'Stock' and file name to Stock.java, updating all references) or update the problem statement and UML to refer to 'Inventory' instead of 'Stock'. Ensure SealSaloon and tests consistently use the same type name.
